verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed{H4899}, full{H4392} of the Spirit{H7307} the Holy{H6944}, departed{H5265} from the Yarden{H3383} and was led{H5090} by{H1157} the Spirit{H7307} into the wilderness{H4057}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נסע (nasa', H5265) meaning 'to pull up tent-pins, depart on a journey' — this specific Hebrew term for departure carries the nomadic sense of breaking camp and beginning a journey, connecting to Israel's wilderness wanderings. Greek ὑπέστρεψεν means 'returned,' but Hebrew emphasizes departure/beginning.
greek_deviations: Hebrew emphasizes departure (נסע 'departed') from the Jordan, while Greek emphasizes return (ὑπέστρεψεν 'returned') from the Jordan.
translation_notes: 'The Anointed' for משיח preserves the Hebrew messianic terminology.
'Departed' for נסע captures the sense of setting out on a journey.

verses.translation: And remaining{H5975} there{H8033} forty{H705} days{H3117} and being tested{H5254} by{H1157} YHWH{H3068}, and he did not{H3808} eat{H398} until{H5704} [the] forty{H705} days{H3117}. And when{H834} those forty{H705} days{H3117} had passed{H5674}, Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed{H4899} was hungry{H7456}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יהוה (YHWH, H3068) — the divine name. Greek has τοῦ διαβόλου ('the devil'). This is a major theological difference: Hebrew attributes the testing to YHWH directly, while Greek attributes it to the devil. This reflects the Hebrew understanding that YHWH tests his servants (as with Abraham, Job), following OT precedent.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tested by YHWH' (ונתנסה בעד יהוה). Greek: 'tested by the devil' (πειραζόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ διαβόλου). Completely different theological framing of who conducts the test.
translation_notes: YHWH preserved as the Hebrew divine name rather than translating as 'the LORD'.
The Hebrew presents YHWH as the one conducting the test, consistent with OT theology where God tests his servants.
textual_notes: The phrase א רְבּעים appears to be a scribal error or variant spelling for ארבעים (forty).

verses.translation: And the Satan{H7854} came{H935} to him and said{H559} to him, 'If{H518} you{H859} are the son{H1121} of God{H410} the Living{H2416}, say{H559} to these{H431} stones{H68} that they should become{H7725} bread{H3899}.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses השטן (ha-satan, H7854) with the definite article — 'the Satan' as a title/office, consistent with Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1-2. The Hebrew presents Satan as a specific adversary figure, not merely 'the devil.'

Uses אל חי (El Chai) — 'God the Living' (H410 + H2416). This is the classical Hebrew designation for the living God as opposed to dead idols, found throughout the OT (Deut 5:26, Josh 3:10, 1 Sam 17:26, Ps 42:2). Greek θεοῦ lacks this specific 'Living' emphasis.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'God the Living' (אל חי). Greek: simply 'God' (τοῦ Θεοῦ) without the 'Living' qualifier.
Hebrew: 'stones' (plural אבנַים). Greek: 'stone' (singular λίθῳ).
translation_notes: 'The Satan' preserves the Hebrew title with definite article.
'God the Living' captures the Hebrew emphasis on the living God versus dead idols.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} answered{H6030}, 'It is written{H3789} that man{H120} does not{H3808} live{H2416} by{H5921} bread{H3899} alone{H905}, but{H3588} rather{H518} by every{H3605} word{H1697} that goes forth{H3318} from the mouth{H6310} of YHWH{H3068}.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses יהוה (YHWH, H3068) — the divine name, not found in the Greek text. Greek has simply θεοῦ ('God'), but Hebrew specifically invokes the covenant name of Israel's God, connecting this to Deuteronomy 8:3 which also uses יהוה.
greek_deviations: Hebrew includes the full quotation ending 'from the mouth of YHWH' while Greek text is truncated, ending at 'by bread alone.'
translation_notes: YHWH preserved as the Hebrew divine name.
The Hebrew provides the complete quotation from Deuteronomy 8:3.
textual_notes: This appears to quote Deuteronomy 8:3 more completely than the Greek parallel.

verses.translation: And the Satan{H7854} led{H5090} Yeshua{H3442} to a mountain{H2022}, one{H259} very{H3966} great{H1419}, and showed{H7200} him all{H3605} the kingdoms{H4438} of the world{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכוּת (malkhut, H4438) — 'kingdoms/dominions' — the Hebrew royal terminology for sovereign rule. This is the standard OT word for kingdom, connecting to David's kingdom, God's kingdom, etc. Greek βασιλείας conveys similar meaning but Hebrew malkhut carries the full weight of OT kingdom theology.

Uses עוֹלם (olam, H5769) — 'world/eternity' — which in Hebrew can mean both spatial (world) and temporal (eternity/age) dimensions. Greek οἰκουμένης specifically means 'inhabited world' (more geographical), while Hebrew olam has broader cosmic-temporal meaning.
greek_deviations: Greek includes the phrase 'in a moment of time' (ἐν στιγμῇ χρόνου) which is absent from the Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'The Satan' preserves the Hebrew title with definite article.
'Kingdoms' for malkhut connects to OT royal theology.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to him, 'Behold{H2009}, I will give{H5414} to you all{H3605} these{H428} matters{H6045}.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַנּה (hinneh, H2009) — 'behold!' — the classical Hebrew attention-getting particle found throughout the OT in divine and prophetic speech. This Hebrew interjection carries more dramatic weight than a simple statement.
greek_deviations: Hebrew is much shorter and lacks the Greek expansion about the authority being delivered to Satan and his power to give it to whomever he wishes.
translation_notes: 'Behold' preserves the dramatic Hebrew interjection hinneh.

verses.translation: If{H518} you will fall{H5307} at my feet{H7273} and worship{H6419} me.
Yeshua{H3442} answered{H6030} and said{H559} to him, 'It is written{H3789}: The Lord{H113} your God{H430} you shall worship{H6419}, and him you shall serve{H5647}.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses האדוֹן (ha-adon, H113) — 'the Lord/Master' — the Hebrew title of sovereignty, distinct from יהוה. This term emphasizes God's lordship and authority, commonly used in the OT for both human and divine masters.
greek_deviations: Hebrew lacks the phrase 'Get behind me, Satan' found in the Greek text.
translation_notes: 'The Lord' for ha-adon distinguishes this from YHWH.
The Hebrew provides a direct quotation from Deuteronomy 6:13.

verses.translation: Then{H227} he brought{H5927} him to the holy{H6918} city{H5892} and set{H5117} him upon the highest{H3148} place{H4725} of the temple{H4720}. And the Satan{H7854} said{H559} to him, 'If{H518} you{H859} are{H1931} the son{H1121} of God{H433}, cast{H5307} yourself{H6106} [down].'

one_way_hebrew: Uses אלוֹהּ (eloah, H433) — the singular form of God found primarily in Job (41 times) and poetic passages (Deut 32:15,17; Hab 3:3). A back-translator from Greek θεοῦ would typically use אלהים (Elohim, H430), not this rare singular poetic form.

Uses העיר הקדושה ('the holy city') — a specific Hebrew designation for Jerusalem, emphasizing its sacred character. This phrase appears in Isaiah 48:2, 52:1 and connects to the OT understanding of Jerusalem's holiness.
translation_notes: 'The holy city' captures the Hebrew emphasis on Jerusalem's sacred character.
Eloah represents the rare singular form of God, distinct from the common Elohim.

verses.translation: For{H3588} it is written{H3789}: He{H1931} will command{H6680} his angels{H4397} concerning you that they should guard{H8104} you.

textual_notes: The final character appears to be a quotation mark or textual notation.

verses.translation: In [their] hands{H3027} they will bear{H5375} you, lest{H6435} you strike{H5062} your foot{H7272} against a stone{H68}.

textual_notes: This continues the quotation from Psalm 91:11-12.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to him, '[Away with] these{H428}!' And he said{H559}, 'It is spoken{H1696} another{H312} time{H6471}: You shall not{H3808} test{H5254} the Lord{H113} YHWH{H3068} your God{H430}.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses the full divine title האדון יהוה אלהיך ('the Lord YHWH your God') combining three divine names/titles. Greek has only Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου ('Lord your God'). The Hebrew preserves the complete covenantal formula including the sacred name יהוה, showing closer adherence to the OT source (Deut 6:16).
Uses דבר פעם אחרת ('spoken another time') — a Hebrew legal formula indicating a second witness or repeated commandment, emphasizing the authority of repeated divine speech.
greek_deviations: Hebrew includes the complete divine title 'the Lord YHWH your God' while Greek has only 'Lord your God' without YHWH.
Hebrew has an interjection 'these!' (האלה) not present in Greek.
translation_notes: The Hebrew preserves the full covenantal name structure from Deuteronomy.
'These!' appears to be an exclamation of dismissal.

verses.translation: And when all{H3605} the testing{H5254} was completed{H7999}, the tester{H5254} departed{H5265} from him, and [he] left{H5117} Yeshua{H3442} alone. And the angels{H4397} approached{H5066} him and ministered{H8334} to Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המנסה (ha-menasseh, H5254) — 'the tester' — a participle form that identifies Satan by his function as the one who tests, rather than as 'devil' (διάβολος). This connects to the OT understanding of testing/proving, as in God testing Abraham or Job being tested.

Uses נסע (nasa', H5265) again for departure — the same term used in v.1, creating a literary bracket around the temptation narrative. The Satan 'departs on a journey' just as Yeshua earlier 'departed on a journey' from the Jordan.
greek_deviations: Hebrew explicitly mentions the angels ministering 'to Yeshua the Anointed,' while Greek ends more simply.
Greek includes 'for a season' (ἄχρι καιροῦ) which is absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'The tester' for ha-menasseh identifies Satan functionally rather than by title.
The repetition of nasa' creates literary structure in the Hebrew narrative.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed{H4899} returned{H7725} in the power{H3581} of the Spirit{H7307} to Galilee{H1552}, and his report{H8088} went out{H3318} throughout all{H3605} the land{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֹח (koach, H3581) — 'power/strength' — the Hebrew word for physical and spiritual strength, often used of divine power in the OT (as in Zechariah 4:6 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit'). Greek δύναμις conveys similar meaning but koach has more concrete, physical connotations in Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Greek has περιχώρου ('surrounding region') while Hebrew has simply ארץ ('land').
translation_notes: 'Power' for koach connects to OT language about divine strength.
'Report' captures the sense of news spreading about him.

verses.translation: And he{H1931} was teaching{H3925} in their synagogues{H4150} and was exalted{H5927} by{H1157} all{H3605} of them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בבתי כנסיותיהם (be-vattei knesiyyoteihem) — literally 'in their houses of assembly/synagogues.' The Hebrew term כנסיות (knesiyyot) is the plural of כנסת (knesset) meaning 'assembly,' the Hebrew root behind 'synagogue.' This shows the Hebrew text using native Hebrew terminology for Jewish religious institutions.
translation_notes: 'Houses of their synagogues' reflects the Hebrew compound expression.
'Was exalted' for the passive form suggests being glorified or honored.

verses.literal: And he came to Nazareth where he was raised [and entered] according to his custom to [the] house of the assembly on [the] sabbath and he rose rejoicing
verses.amplified: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, [and entered] as was his custom into the house of the assembly [synagogue] on the Sabbath, and he rose up gladly [or: joyfully]
work: לבית (בית): Candidates: H1004 'a house', H1005 same, H1006 'Bajith, a place', H3487 'sign of object'. Chose H1004 because 'house of the assembly' (בית הכנסת) is the standard Hebrew term for synagogue.

שמח: Candidates: H8055 'to brighten up, be blithe', H8056 'blithe or gleeful', H4220 'fat/rich', H4221 'marrow'. The ש prefix is part of the root here. In context of rising in a synagogue, H8056 'gleeful/glad' fits as an adjectival description of his state. H4220/H4221 would require reading שמח as ש+מח which is forced here.
ambiguities: שמח could theoretically be parsed as ש+מח (relative particle + 'fat/marrow'), but this produces a nonsensical reading in context. Reading as the root שמח 'rejoice/glad' is far more coherent. Whether it is a verb (H8055 'he rejoiced') or adjective (H8056 'glad/joyful') is ambiguous; both work contextually.

verses.translation: And they gave{H5414} him{} the scroll{H5612} of Yeshayah{H3470} the prophet{H5030}, and when{H834} he opened{H6605} the scroll{H5612} he found{H4672} the place{H4725} where it was written{}:

one_way_hebrew: Uses ספר (sefer, H5612 — 'scroll/book') consistently for both instances. This is the standard Hebrew term for a written document, particularly sacred texts (Deut 17:18, Josh 1:8). The repetition emphasizes the physical handling of the sacred scroll.
Uses ישׁעיה (Yeshayah, H3470) — the Hebrew form of the prophet's name, not the Hellenized 'Isaiah' that might be expected from a Greek back-translation.
translation_notes: 'Scroll' for ספר rather than 'book' to reflect the ancient format of the text.

verses.translation: The spirit{H7307} of God{H430} is upon me{H5943}, and because of{H5668} this{H2088} he has anointed{H4886} me{} and sent me{} to the poor{} to proclaim good news{} and to heal{H7495} the broken{} of heart{H3820} and to proclaim{} repentance{H8666} to the captives{} and to the blind{} sight{} and to release{} the broken ones{} for forgiveness{}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תּשׁוּבַה (teshuvah, H8666 — 'return/repentance') — the classic Hebrew concept of turning back to God, from שׁוב ('to return'). This carries the full OT meaning of directional return to God's path (1 Kgs 8:33, Jer 3:14). Greek μετάνοια focuses on mental change; Hebrew focuses on directional movement back to God.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spirit of God' (רוּח אלהַֹים). Greek: 'Spirit of the Lord' (Πνεῦμα Κυρίου). Different divine designation.
Hebrew adds 'and to release the broken ones for forgiveness' — an expansion not present in the provided Greek text.
translation_notes: 'Repentance' for תּשׁוּבַה, though the Hebrew literally means 'return' — the act of turning back to God.
textual_notes: This appears to be a citation from Isaiah 61:1-2, adapted in Hebrew.

verses.translation: Proclaiming{} the year{} of the Lord{H113} evening{H6153} and day{H3117} of vengeance{H5359}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אדון (adon, H113 — 'lord/master') rather than יהוה (YHWH). This is the standard Hebrew term for 'lord' used in respectful address, found throughout the OT (Gen 23:6, Exod 21:5). A back-translator from Greek κυρίου might use יהוה, but adon reflects natural Hebrew usage.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'evening and day of vengeance' — the Greek text provided only has 'to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' with no mention of vengeance or evening/day.
translation_notes: ערב can mean 'evening' or 'pleasant' — here taking 'evening' to maintain the temporal parallel with 'day'.
textual_notes: This continues the Isaiah 61 citation, with Hebrew preserving the 'day of vengeance' that the Greek omits.

verses.translation: And when{H834} he finished{} the scroll{H5612} he returned it{} to the minister{H8334} and sat down{H3427}, and all{H3605} who{H834} were{} in the house{H1004} of assembly{} were{} gazing at{} him{}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משׁרת (mesharet, from H8334 שׁרת — 'to minister/serve') for the synagogue attendant. This is the Hebrew term for one who serves in religious capacity (1 Kgs 10:5, Joel 1:9, 1:13). Greek ὑπηρέτῃ ('attendant/officer') is more generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'gazing at him' (מבינים בּוֹ). Greek: 'were fastened on him' (ἦσαν ἀτενίζοντες αὐτῷ). Different descriptions of their attention.

verses.translation: He began{} to say{H559} to them{H1992}: Today{H3117} this{H2088} is fulfilled{} — this{H2063} scripture{} in our ears{}.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} were giving{} testimony{H5715} to him{} and wondering{} at the words{} of grace{H2580} proceeding{} from his mouth{}, and they were saying{}: Is this not{} the son{H1121} of Yosef{H3130}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses עדוּת (edut, H5715 — 'testimony/witness') — the legal Hebrew term for bearing witness (Exod 25:16, Num 17:25). This carries the full OT meaning of formal attestation. Greek ἐμαρτύρουν is semantic equivalent but lacks the legal precision of עדוּת.

Uses חן (chen, H2580 — 'grace/favor') — the classic Hebrew term for divine favor and gracious kindness (Gen 6:8, Exod 33:12). This is the standard Hebrew word throughout the OT for God's gracious disposition.
Uses יוֹסף (Yosef, H3130) — the Hebrew form of Joseph's name, not the Hellenized form that might be expected from a Greek back-translation.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them{H1992}: Truly{} you{H859} will say{} this{H2063} likeness{H8544} — Physician{} heal{H4832} yourself{}. [The] many{} things{} we have heard{} done{H6213} in Capernaum{H3723}, do{} you{H859} likewise{H3651} in your land{}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תּמוּנַה (temunah, H8544 — 'likeness/image/form') for 'proverb' — this is the Hebrew word for a visible form or representation (Num 12:8, Deut 4:12). The Hebrew frames the saying as a 'likeness' or 'representation,' not as a παραβολή ('parable/comparison') as in Greek.

Uses כפר (kefar, H3723 — 'village') in the place name כפר נחום (Capernaum) — this preserves the Hebrew etymology of the town name as 'village of Nachum.' A back-translator might simply transliterate the Greek name.

textual_notes: The text shows some corruption in 'א.מת' and 'שׁ1ַמענוּ' where points or letters appear uncertain.

verses.translation: Many{} widows{} were{} in the days{} of Eliyahu{H453} in Yisrael{H3478} when{H834} the heavens{} were shut up{H6113} three{H8147} years{} and six{} months{}, and when{H834} there was{H1961} great{H1419} famine{H7458} in the land{H776}.

Uses עצר (atzar, H6113 — 'to shut up/restrain') for closing the heavens — this is the biblical Hebrew term for divine withholding of rain (Deut 11:17, 1 Kgs 8:35). A back-translator might use a more general term for 'closed.'

verses.translation: And they arose{} and cast him out{} outside{H2351} the city{H5892} and led him{} to the top{H7218} of the mountains{} upon{H5921} which{} the city{H5892} was built{} in order that{H5668} they might cast him down{}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חוּץ (chutz, H2351 — 'outside/outdoors') for spatial separation from the city. This is the standard Hebrew term for 'outside' a walled area (Gen 19:16, Deut 23:11), emphasizing exclusion from the community.

verses.translation: And he went{H1980} to Kfar{H3723} Nachum{H5151}, a city{H5892} of the Galil{H1552}, and there{H8033} he taught{H3925} them on the sabbath{H7676}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כפר (kfar, H3723 — 'village') in construct with נחום (Nachum, H5151) to form 'Kfar Nachum' (Village of Nachum). This is the Hebrew rendering of Capernaum, preserving the Semitic structure. A back-translator from Greek Καφαρναοὺμ would likely transliterate rather than construct this meaningful Hebrew compound.
Uses נחום (Nachum, H5151) — the Hebrew name meaning 'comfort/consolation', the same name as the prophet Nahum. This connects to the OT prophet tradition rather than merely transliterating the Greek.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוסר (musar — 'teaching/discipline', related to H4148) — the OT wisdom term for moral instruction and discipline (Prov 1:2,7,8; 4:1). This Hebrew educational concept is richer than Greek διδαχή ('teaching'), connecting to the full biblical wisdom tradition.

Uses עוז (oz, H5797 — 'strength/power') — the Hebrew term for divine strength and might (Ps 29:1; 96:7; Isa 40:26). A back-translator from Greek ἐξουσίᾳ ('authority') would more likely use רשות ('authority') or שלטון ('dominion'), not this term for divine strength.
greek_deviations: The Hebrew text appears corrupted with extensive textual issues in the latter portion, making comparison with the Greek difficult.

textual_notes: This verse shows extensive textual problems with apparent scribal interpolations including references to Isaiah, Elijah, ravens, and the widow of Zarephath — likely marginal notes that entered the text.

verses.translation: And a man{H120} one{H259} was{H1961} there who had an unclean spirit, and he was{H1961} in the house{H1004} of assembly and crying out{H6817} with a voice{H6963} great{H1419}.

Uses צועק (tzo'ek — 'crying out', from H6817 צעק) — the Hebrew term for crying out in distress or alarm, often to God (Exod 22:22; Judg 3:9,15). The Hebrew conveys the urgency and desperation more vividly than a simple transliteration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew describes the spirit more briefly, without the Greek specification πνεῦμα δαιμονίου ἀκαθάρτου ('spirit of an unclean demon').

verses.translation: And saying{H559}, 'What{H4100} to you, Yeshua{H3442} of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know that you{H859} are{H1931} the son{H1121} of God{H433}.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses אלוה (eloah, H433) — the singular form of God found primarily in Job and poetic texts (Job 3:4; Deut 32:15,17). A back-translator from Greek θεοῦ would typically use the common אלהים (elohim, H430), not this rare singular form that appears mainly in elevated/poetic contexts.
greek_deviations: Greek calls him 'the Holy One of God' (ὁ Ἅγιος τοῦ Θεοῦ), while Hebrew has 'the son of God' (בן האלוה).
translation_notes: The text appears to have some corruption with unusual markings, but the core message is clear.
textual_notes: Some textual corruption visible with unusual diacritical marks in the manuscript.

verses.literal: And Yeshua whispered to him saying be silent and go out from the man and when he expelled him he entered in [the] midst of [the] house of the assembly he went out from him and did not harm him [at] all
verses.amplified: And Yeshua rebuked [or: whispered to] him, saying, Be silent and come out from the man! And when he drove him out, he [the unclean spirit] entered into the midst of the house of the assembly [synagogue], went out from him, and did not harm him [in any] thing
work: האדם: Candidates: H119 'to flush/turn rosy', H120 'a human being', H121 'Adam', H122 'rosy', H123 'Edom', H124 'ruby'. With the definite article ה and in context of an exorcism command 'go out from the man,' H120 'human being' is the clear fit.
בית (H1004): Same reasoning as section 1 — 'house of the assembly' = synagogue.
יצא: H3318 and H3319 are essentially the same ('to go out'). Chose H3318 as the primary entry.

דבר: Candidates: H1696 'to speak', H1697 'a word/thing/matter', H1698 'pestilence', H1699 'pasture'. In the phrase 'did not harm him דבר,' it functions as an adverbial accusative meaning 'a thing' i.e. 'at all / anything.' H1697 fits perfectly.
ambiguities: The sequence 'נכנס באמצע בית הכנסת יצא ממנו' is syntactically ambiguous: it could mean (a) the spirit threw the man into the midst of the synagogue, then went out, or (b) the spirit entered the midst then exited. The lack of explicit subject markers makes the referent uncertain.
לחשו could derive from לחש 'to whisper/charm/rebuke' — the exact nuance (gentle whisper vs. authoritative rebuke) is unclear from consonants alone.
ה!ז!יקו appears to be a damaged form of הזיקו 'harmed him' from the root נזק or הזק.

verses.literal: And all of them feared and [were] speaking among them and saying what word [is] this that there is to him power and command [over] the spirits the evil and they go out from the people
verses.amplified: And all of them were struck with fear and were speaking among themselves and saying: What manner of word [or: matter] is this, that he has power and authority [to] command the evil spirits, and they come out from the people [or: from human beings]?
work: דבר: Candidates: H1696 'to speak', H1697 'a word/matter/thing', H1698 'pestilence', H1699 'pasture'. In 'what דבר is this,' it clearly functions as a noun meaning 'word' or 'matter.' H1697.
הוא: Candidates: H1931 'he/it', H1932 same, H1933 'to be', H1934 'to exist'. Functions as a copula 'is' in the phrase 'what word is this.' H1931.
זה: Candidates: H2088 'this', H2089 'a sheep', H2090 'this or that'. In 'what word is this,' H2088 demonstrative 'this' is the natural reading.

שיש: Candidates: H7893 'marble', H3426 'there is/are'. Reading as ש+יש (relative particle + 'there is') produces 'that there is to him power' = 'that he has power.' H7893 'marble' makes no sense here.
ומצוה: Candidates: H4687 'a command/authority', H6680 'to constitute/enjoin'. As a noun with ו conjunction, H4687 'command/authority' pairs naturally with כח 'power.'
ambiguities: The ים tokens appear as separate words in the manuscript but function as plural suffixes on the preceding words (מדברים, אומרים, יוצאים, אנשים). This may reflect a scribal convention or manuscript damage.
הא%נש!ים appears partially damaged; reading as אנשים 'people/men' based on context.

verses.literal: And his report was spreading in every place of the kingdom
verses.amplified: And the report about him [or: his fame] was being spread [scattered] throughout every place of the region [or: kingdom]
work: היה: Candidates: H1961 'to exist/be/become', H1962 'ruin', H3050 'Jah'. In 'his report היה spreading,' H1961 'was' functions as auxiliary. H1962 'ruin' and H3050 'Jah' make no contextual sense.
מקום: Candidates: H4725 'a place/locality', H6965 'to rise', H6966 same. As a noun following בכל 'in every,' H4725 'place' is the natural reading.
המלכות: H4438 'a rule/dominion' with definite article. Fits as 'the kingdom/region.'
ambiguities: ושמעו could be parsed as 'and they heard him' (verb + suffix) or 'and his report/fame' (noun + possessive suffix). Context of spreading throughout the kingdom favors the noun reading 'his fame/report.'

verses.literal: And Yeshua went out from [the] house of the assembly and entered in [the] house of Shimon and [the] mother-in-law of Shimon was sick from fever great and they entreated his face on her behalf
verses.amplified: And Yeshua went out from the house of the assembly [synagogue] and entered into the house of Shimon [Simon], and Shimon's mother-in-law was ill with a severe [or: great] fever, and they implored him [lit: entreated his face] on her behalf
work: ש!מעון: The consonants ש+מעון could yield: (a) ש (relative particle 'of/that') + מעון H4583 'abode/dwelling', or (b) שמעון H8095 'Shimon.' With בבית preceding it, 'in the house of Shimon' makes perfect narrative sense, and the second שמעון confirms the name. Chose H8095.
שמעון: Candidates: H8095 'Shimon', H4583 'abode', H4584 'Maon', H5770 'to watch', H5771 'evil'. As a proper name following וחמות 'mother-in-law of,' H8095 'Shimon' is clearly correct.
גדול: H1419 'great.' Modifies קדחת 'fever' — 'a great fever' meaning severe.
ambiguities: The first ש!מעון is split as ש! + מעון in the manuscript, which could technically be read as 'that/of' + 'dwelling/abode' (H4583). However, the parallel with the full שמעון later in the verse confirms this is the name Shimon (Simon).
וחילו could derive from חלה 'to entreat/beseech' (they besought) or חיל 'to writhe/tremble.' Context of petitioning on behalf of a sick person favors 'they entreated.'

verses.literal: [He] stood over her commanded to [the] fever that it should leave her and immediately she rose and she served them
verses.amplified: He stood over her [and] commanded the fever to leave her, and immediately she rose up and began serving them
work: עמד: Candidates: H5975 'to stand', H5976 'to shake', H5977 'a spot', H5978 'along with'. In context of approaching a sick person, 'he stood' (H5975) is the natural action — he stood over her. Testing H5978 'along with her' is possible but H5975 better matches עליה 'over her.'

עליה: H5944 'something lofty/upper room.' However, with the preposition על + suffix הּ, this reads 'over her / upon her,' which fits perfectly with עמד 'he stood over her.' The Strong's entry H5944 refers to the noun עלייה 'upper room,' but here the consonants match על+יה (preposition + suffix).
ומיד: From יד H3027 'hand.' With prefix ו+מ, this reads 'and from hand' = 'immediately' (an idiomatic usage of מיד).
קמה: H7054 'a stalk of grain.' However, the consonants קמה also represent the verb קום 'to rise' with feminine 3rd person suffix — 'she rose.' Context demands the verbal reading.
ambiguities: עליה: The consonants match both על+יה 'over her' (preposition + pronominal suffix) and עליה H5944 'upper room.' Context clearly demands 'over her.'
קמה: H7054 'stalk of grain' shares consonants with the verb form 'she rose' from קום. The narrative context (recovering from fever, then serving) unambiguously demands 'she rose.'

לה could refer to the woman ('to her') or to the fever ('to it,' feminine in Hebrew). In context of commanding the fever, it likely means 'he commanded it (the fever)' or possibly 'he commanded [regarding] her — to the fever.'

verses.literal: And when came the sun all those who were there sick of various illnesses they brought them to him and he placing upon them his hands and healing them
verses.amplified: And when the sun was setting [or: came down], all those who had [people] there sick with various [or: different] illnesses brought them to him, and he was laying his hands upon them and healing them
work: וכאשר: From אשר. Candidates include H833 'to be straight/happy', H834 'who/which/when', H835 'happiness', H836 'Asher', H837 'happiness', H838 'a step'. With כ prefix and ו conjunction, כאשר = 'when/as' — H834 is the clear choice.

והבקר: Candidates: H1239 'to plough/inspect', H1240 same, H1241 'cattle', H1242 'morning/dawn'. Wait — the consonants in the source are ה<מש not בקר. The word list entry says והבקר but the actual text has implied 'the sun.' Reading ה<מש as השמש 'the sun' with damage. The word list heading says והבקר but context suggests this is about sunset.
שם: Candidates: H8033 'there', H8034 'name/reputation', H8035 'Shem', H8036 same as H8034. In 'who were שם sick' — 'who were there sick' (H8033) is the natural reading.
והוא: H1931 'he' — emphatic pronoun 'and he [himself]' was laying hands.
במדבר in this section is not present, disregard.
ambiguities: ה<מש appears to be a damaged form; likely השמש 'the sun.' The heading word והבקר with candidates for בקר (H1242 'morning') conflicts with the consonantal text which seems to reference the sun setting. This may reflect manuscript corruption or a compound expression.
חףליים appears damaged; likely חלאים or חליים 'illnesses/diseases.'
מחלופי is unusual; it seems to mean 'of various kinds / different types' — possibly from the root חלף 'to change/exchange,' hence 'varying/different.'
ע ליהם appears to be עליהם 'upon them' split across a line or damaged.

verses.translation: And demons came out from many, crying out and saying, 'You{H859} are{H1931} the Anointed{H4899}, son{H1121} of God{H433}.' And he rebuked them because{H3588} they knew that he{H1931} was the Anointed{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משיח (mashiach, H4899 — 'anointed one/Messiah') — the Hebrew technical term for the anointed king/priest/prophet, particularly the coming Davidic king (1 Sam 2:10; Ps 2:2; Dan 9:25,26). This is the precise Hebrew messianic title, not a transliteration of Greek Χριστός.
Uses אלוה (eloah, H433) again — the singular poetic form of God, reinforcing this stylistic preference throughout the text.
greek_deviations: Hebrew identifies him as 'the Anointed, son of God' while Greek has 'Son of God' in the first instance and 'the Anointed' in the second.

verses.literal: And the morning light he went out from them and was going in the wilderness and the peoples searching [for] him and they came to him and holding on to him that not he should separate from them
verses.amplified: And at the light of morning [dawn], he went out from them and traveled into the wilderness [or: open land], and the people were searching for him and came to him and were holding onto him so that he would not depart from them
work: והבקר: Candidates: H1239 'to plough/inspect', H1240 same, H1241 'cattle', H1242 'morning/dawn'. Paired with אור 'light,' the phrase 'the morning light' = dawn. H1242 is the clear choice.
אור: Candidates: H215 'to be luminous', H216 'illumination/light', H217 'flame/East', H218 'Ur (place)'. Following בקר 'morning,' H216 'light/illumination' creates 'morning light' = dawn.

במדבר: Candidates: H4057 'pasture/desert/wilderness', H1696 'to speak', H1697 'word', H1698 'pestilence', H1699 'pasture'. With prefix ב 'in' and context of going to a solitary place, H4057 'wilderness/open land' is correct.
ובאו: The candidate listed is H176 'or/if' for או, but ובאו is clearly ו+באו from בוא 'to come' — 'and they came.' The Strong's candidate for או is irrelevant here.
מהם: Candidates: H1990 'Ham', H1991 'wealth', H1992 'they'. With prefix מ 'from,' this is מ+הם = 'from them.' H1992 'they' with the preposition.
ambiguities: מ<ם appears damaged; likely מהם 'from them' or משם 'from there.' Context of departing favors 'from them.'
עדיו could be parsed as עד+יו 'to him' (preposition + suffix) or as a form related to עדה 'assembly.' The former fits the narrative of people coming to him.

verses.literal: And to them he said [it is] obligated for him to declare to towns other [the] kingdom of God for on account of this I was sent
verses.amplified: And to them he said: It is necessary [or: obligatory] for me to proclaim [or: declare] to other towns the kingdom of God, for on account of this I was sent
words: on account of / for the sake of
work: אמר: Candidates: H559 'to say', H560 same, H561 'something said', H562 same, H563 'a lamb', H564 'Immer (name)'. As a verb following 'to them,' H559 'he said' is the obvious reading.
מלכות: Candidates: H4438 'a rule/dominion', H3575 'Cuth (place)'. In the phrase 'kingdom of God,' H4438 is clearly correct.

האל: Candidates: H408 'not', H409 same, H410 'strength/Almighty/deity', H411 'these/those', H412 same, H413 'to/near'. With definite article ה and following מלכות, 'the God / the Mighty One' (H410) is the clear reading — 'the kingdom of God.'
כי: Candidates: H3587 'a brand/scar', H3588 'conjunction: for/because/that'. As a causal conjunction introducing the reason, H3588.
בעבור: Candidates: H5668 'on account of / in order that', H5669 'stored grain.' In 'for on account of this I was sent,' H5668 is correct.
זה: Candidates: H2088 'this', H2089 'a sheep', H2090 'this/that'. In 'on account of this,' H2088 demonstrative 'this' is the natural reading.

להגיד: The candidate H1517 גיד 'a thong/tendon' shares consonants, but להגיד is clearly the hiphil infinitive of נגד 'to declare/tell.' The Strong's list only offered H1517 for גיד, but the verb form הגיד derives from נגד (H5046). Context of proclaiming the kingdom demands 'to declare.'
ambiguities: להגיד: The only Strong's candidate offered (H1517 'tendon/thong') does not fit. This is the hiphil infinitive construct of נגד 'to tell/declare' (H5046), which was not listed among candidates. The reading 'to declare/proclaim' is certain from context.

לו 'for him' vs. 'for me' — since Yeshua is the speaker, this likely means 'for me' (using the third person in self-reference or a scribal convention), or it is an indirect construction 'it is obligated for him' in the narrator's framing of the quote.

verses.translation: And he was{H1961} preaching in the houses of assembly of the Galil{H1552}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בתי כנסיות (batei knesiyot — 'houses of assemblies') — the plural Hebrew construction for synagogues, literally 'houses of gatherings'. This is natural Hebrew synagogue terminology, not a back-translation.
greek_deviations: Greek text says 'synagogues of Judaea' (συναγωγὰς τῆς Ἰουδαίας) while Hebrew has 'synagogues of the Galil' (בתי כנסיות של גלילה).
